doc.title: Warren Bernhardt interviewed by Monk Rowe, Bearsville, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Early New York money and the family piano
summary: Pay at the Vanguard and his cheap rent, plus the story of his grandfather's piano that brought his parents together.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Was he struggling financially too? I mean the fact that he had three or four albums out maybe didn’t necessarily translate to checks.

Well by the sixties he was doing okay. He still didn’t have Helen Keane as a manager yet, but he was doing okay. I mean he’d won all the awards already. The Down Beat Critics Poll and the Popular Poll, which in those days was a big deal. It assured that you could get work everywhere. Work didn’t pay much, I remember the Vanguard paid eighty-six dollars a week for a sideman, and twice that much for the leader in those days. But you could live on that. My rent was a hundred dollars a month for a whole floor of a brownstone. I mean you managed to do it with my piano here. That was with me for that whole time.
This piano behind you has followed you around?

It was my grandfather’s. It’s the reason I’m here. Oh that’s another story, that goes way back. My mother talked her father into buying a piano so that Larry Bernhardt would come over and play the piano for them because my grandfather was a music lover. His name was Warren too. And so that was her thing. And then she said, “Can I take music lessons with Larry?” And I think they worked on one Chopin prelude, that was it, and then they were married soon thereafter. So this piano is a present, and I inherited it later.
Yeah the piano is inextricably involved. That was a whole other thing, that gets into the whole synthesizer trip which I tried. Now I pretty much am back to the piano.
